historical_core: Plural postwar modernisms centered roughly on the mid-1940s through mid-1960s.
Material and production experiments joined craft, industry, architecture, communication, and everyday use.
Good Design programs, Case Study housing, tract development, corporate planning, and collaborative total environments are distinct evidence threads.
current_expressions: Warm, layered, collected rooms combining vintage and contemporary pieces.
Dark woods, deeper upholstery, oversized art, and richer textiles.
Explicitly labeled late-1960s or 1970s-adjacent earth tones and lounge forms.
composition: Readable circulation with low horizontal masses and activity zones.
Indoor–outdoor sightlines where the actual architecture supports them.
Rugs, storage, hearths, screens, or lighting used to zone open space.
furniture_forms: Shaped plywood, upholstered rectilinear volumes, wire shells, slender metal frames, and component storage.
Human scale and visible construction matter more than iconic silhouette.
Mix authentic vintage, licensed production, and well-made compatible contemporary pieces.
materials: Plywood, solid wood, fiberglass, metal, wire, glass, brick, stone, cork, terrazzo, laminate, and textiles.
Contrast soft and hard or opaque and transparent according to use.
Prefer repairable construction over disposable decorative veneer.
palette: Neutral architectural fields with saturated or textile-led color.
Pale and dark woods, black frames, brick, cork, and multi-color pattern.
Olive, rust, ochre, tobacco, and cream belong to current or 1970s-adjacent expressions when named.
lighting: Daylight and landscape views organize space where available.
Layer pendants, adjustable task lights, wall light, and low pools of warm illumination.
Control glare and meet actual reading, screen, work, and safety needs.
textiles_art: Use rugs, upholstery, curtains, art, ceramics, books, plants, and personal collections as lived layers.
Let textiles provide zoning, acoustics, pattern, or the strongest color.
Contextualize non-Western objects rather than using them as anonymous cosmopolitan markers.
spatial_density: Keep furniture hierarchy and clear movement while allowing meaningful collection.
Use closed storage to support calm without erasing hobbies or work.
Ask the user which belongings should remain visible.
variants: California Case Study and desert modernism.
Tract-house modernism and corporate Planning Unit interiors.
Regional and international modernisms; Danish Modern and high modernism remain distinct overlaps.
questions: Do the references indicate historical postwar design or a warmer current collected usage?
Which signals matter most: low proportion, material contrast, art, glazing, color, or particular objects?
Are 1970s-adjacent colors and lounge forms welcome, uncertain, or rejected?
Which existing furniture, access needs, and activities must lead?
cliches_to_avoid: Tapered legs, walnut, starbursts, and Mad Men as a sufficient definition.
A white affluent male-designer canon that erases race, gender, labor, and marketing.
Calling every warm-wood current room historically exact.
positive_prompt_guidance: Describe spatial hierarchy, human scale, production logic, material contrast, lighting, and chosen current-versus-historical register.
Name the user's retained objects and desired level of collection.
Specify one or two evidence-led signals instead of stacking retro tokens.
negative_prompt_guidance: Avoid generic Mad Men sets, starburst décor, logo-like icon piles, and default orange-and-teal grading.
Avoid empty luxury staging that removes books, art, work, and personal evidence.
Do not replace user requirements with low seating or period replicas.
